light-cahill:
How to tie a Light Cahill. This pale Catskill dry has been matching cream and sulphur-colored mayflies for more than a century. Its wood duck wings and ginger hackle make it a classic worth learning.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size twelve to eighteen. Cream eight-oh thread. Wood duck flank for the wings, light ginger fibers for the tail, cream dubbing for the body, and a light ginger or cream rooster hackle.

Step one. A third back from the eye, tie in a bunch of wood duck fibers. Stand them upright and divide them into two wings with figure-eight wraps.

Step two. At the bend, tie in a tail of light ginger fibers, about as long as the shank.

Step three. Dub a slim, tapered cream body up to the wings.

Step four. Tie in the hackle and wind it, a few turns behind the wings and a few in front. Tie it off and whip finish.

Fish it at dusk on summer evenings, when pale mayflies come off the water.

x-caddis:
How to tie an X-Caddis. Craig Mathews and John Juracek designed this caddis to ride low in the film, trailing its shuck like an insect that's still hatching. With no hackle, it fools the fussiest trout.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size twelve to twenty. Tan eight-oh thread. Amber or olive Z-Lon for the shuck, fine dubbing to match the body, and fine deer hair for the wing.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a short tuft of Z-Lon as the trailing shuck.

Step two. Dub a slim body forward, stopping about a quarter of the shank behind the eye.

Step three. Clean and stack a small bunch of deer hair, and tie it in on top so it flares slightly. The tips should reach the bend.

Step four. Trim the hair butts into a small head and whip finish.

Fish it to fussy trout that are eating caddis emergers in the film, especially on smooth water.

klinkhamer-special:
How to tie a Klinkhamer Special. Hans van Klinken's emerger hangs its body below the surface while the hackle and post float above. Selective trout and grayling see a bug that's caught halfway out of the water.

You'll need a curved emerger hook, size ten to eighteen. Grey eight-oh thread. White or orange poly yarn for the post, tan or olive dubbing for the abdomen, peacock herl for the thorax, and a light dun or chestnut hackle.

Step one. Near the front of the hook, tie in a poly post, angled slightly forward, and stiffen its base with thread.

Step two. Dub a slim abdomen that runs well down around the bend of the hook.

Step three. Wrap a short thorax of peacock herl around the base of the post.

Step four. Tie in the hackle and wind it around the post, parachute style. Tie it off and whip finish.

It's excellent for selective trout and grayling during caddis and mayfly hatches.

blue-winged-olive-parachute:
How to tie a Blue Winged Olive Parachute. Small olive mayflies hatch in spring and fall, often on grey, drizzly days. This little parachute sits low like a real dun, and the post makes it easy to follow.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size sixteen to twenty-two. Olive eight-oh thread. Grey or white poly yarn for the post, dun microfibbets for the tail, olive-grey fine dubbing for the body, and a dun hackle.

Step one. A third back from the eye, tie in the poly post and stand it up with thread wraps around its base.

Step two. At the bend, tie in a few microfibbets as the tail.

Step three. Dub a slim, tapered body up to the post.

Step four. Tie in the hackle at the post, and wind it down the post three to five turns.

Step five. Tie off the hackle under the post, add a little dubbing in front, and whip finish.

Fish it to rising trout on overcast spring and autumn days.

hippie-stomper:
How to tie a Hippie Stomper. Andrew Grillos's little foam attractor has a flashy body, a white wing post and wiggly legs. It floats all day and trout eat it like candy in the summer.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size ten to sixteen. Black six-oh thread. Moose hair for the tail, peacock or other flashy dubbing for the body, a strip of two-millimeter foam, white calf or Para Post for the wing, and rubber legs.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a short tail of moose hair, then the foam strip.

Step two. Dub a flashy body forward, then pull the foam over the top and tie it down near the front.

Step three. At that tie-down point, add the white wing on top and a pair of rubber legs on each side.

Step four. Trim the foam and whip finish.

Fish it as a summer attractor, or as the float for a dry-dropper rig.

goddard-caddis:
How to tie a Goddard Caddis. John Goddard and Cliff Henry's caddis is made almost entirely of spun deer hair, clipped into a tent shape. It's practically unsinkable, and perfect for skating across the surface.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size ten to sixteen. Strong grey three-oh thread. Deer hair for the body and wing, a brown rooster hackle, and two hackle stems for the antennae.

Step one. Spin several small bunches of deer hair over most of the shank, packing each one back tight.

Step two. Trim the hair into a caddis tent shape: flat underneath, and sloping up to a peak at the back.

Step three. At the front, tie in two stripped hackle stems as antennae, then wind a few turns of brown hackle.

Step four. Tie off the hackle and whip finish.

Skate it across a riffle or a lake in the evening, when the caddis are active.

amys-ant:
How to tie an Amy's Ant. Jack Dennis's big foam bug has a sparkly chenille body, an elk hair wing and rubber legs. It can pass for a hopper, a cricket or a stonefly, and it floats a nymph all day.

You'll need a two-X-long dry hook, size six to twelve. Tan three-oh thread. Crystal chenille for the body, a strip of two-millimeter foam for the back, elk hair with a little flash for the wing, and rubber legs.

Step one. Start the thread and wrap a crystal chenille body along the shank.

Step two. Lay the foam on top and tie it down in segments as you go, so the back looks jointed.

Step three. At the front, add an elk hair wing with a little flash, and rubber legs on each side.

Step four. Fold the foam forward to form a head, tie it down, and whip finish.

Fish it as a hopper, cricket or stonefly, or use it as an indicator dry with a nymph underneath.

parachute-ant:
How to tie a Parachute Ant. Ants fall into the water all summer long, and trout love them. This version has two dubbed humps and a bright post at the waist, so you can actually see it on the water.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size fourteen to twenty. Black eight-oh thread. Black or cinnamon dubbing for the body, bright poly yarn for the post, and a black or grizzly hackle.

Step one. At the back of the hook, dub a round hump for the ant's rear end.

Step two. At the waist, tie in a short post of bright poly, then wind a few turns of hackle around it, parachute style.

Step three. Dub a smaller front hump between the hackle and the eye, and whip finish.

Drop it along the banks on summer days, especially when there's a breeze.

foam-beetle:
How to tie a Foam Beetle. A black foam shell over a peacock herl body makes a simple beetle that floats like a cork. Trout under overhanging trees eat beetles all summer long.

You'll need a standard dry hook, size twelve to eighteen. Black six-oh thread. A strip of black two-millimeter foam for the shell, peacock herl for the body, fine black rubber legs, and a small orange or yellow foam dot as a sighter.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a strip of black foam, pointing back.

Step two. Tie in a few strands of peacock herl and wind a full body forward.

Step three. Pull the foam over the top and tie it down near the eye, leaving a short head of foam in front.

Step four. Add a rubber leg on each side, and a small bright foam dot on top so you can see it.

Splat it down under overhanging trees on summer days.

sparkle-dun:
How to tie a Sparkle Dun. Craig Mathews added a sparkling trailing shuck to the Comparadun, and created one of the best mayfly patterns for smooth water. It rides low in the film, just like a hatching dun.

You'll need a standard dry fly hook, size twelve to twenty-two. Eight-oh thread to match the body. Fine comparadun deer hair for the wing, Z-Lon or sparkle yarn for the shuck, and fine dubbing to match the hatch.

Step one. Stack a bunch of comparadun hair and tie it in a third back from the eye, with the tips pointing forward. Trim the butts at an angle.

Step two. At the bend, tie in a short tuft of Z-Lon as the shuck.

Step three. Dub a slim body forward to the wing.

Step four. Push the wing upright with thread wraps in front of it, then dub around the base so it fans out in a half circle.

Step five. Whip finish.

Match the color to the hatch, like PMDs, olives or tricos, and fish it to rising trout on smooth water.
